theme: Walk in love; household codes; the armor of God
readingInstruction: Read Ephesians 5:1-6:24. This long reading continues the practical section: walking in love and light, being filled with the Spirit, relationships in the household, and the armor of God. Read with care, as Paul’s teaching on marriage is both beautiful and debated. Read the armor of God as an invitation to stand.
settingTheScene: Paul continues his instructions for the Christian life. He starts with imitating God and walking in love, then describes life in the Spirit, then addresses relationships in the household: wives and husbands, children and parents, slaves and masters. Finally he turns to spiritual warfare. The household instructions were countercultural. Husbands are told to love like Christ; children, wives, and slaves are addressed as moral agents; masters are warned that they have a Master in heaven.
observation: “And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God” (5:2).
“And do not get drunk with wine, for that is debauchery, but be filled with the Spirit” (5:18).
“Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” (5:21).
“Husbands, love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her” (5:25).
“Finally, be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might” (6:10).
“For we do not wrestle against flesh and blood, but against the rulers, against the authorities, against the cosmic powers over this present darkness” (6:12).
“And take the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (6:17).
“Praying at all times in the Spirit, with all prayer and supplication” (6:18).
interpretation:
“Therefore be imitators of God, as beloved children. And walk in love, as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us.” The pattern for the Christian life is God’s own love in Christ. Paul warns against sexual immorality, impurity, covetousness, and obscene talk, which are not fitting among saints. “For at one time you were darkness, but now you are light in the Lord. Walk as children of light.” Light exposes darkness and shows what pleases the Lord.

“Be filled with the Spirit.” This is a command in the present tense, meaning to keep being filled. It is contrasted with drunkenness: instead of being controlled by wine, be controlled by the Spirit. The results are described in participles: speaking to one another in psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing and making melody to the Lord, giving thanks, and submitting to one another. A Spirit-filled life is marked by worship, gratitude, and mutual submission.

Then the household. “Submitting to one another out of reverence for Christ” introduces the passage. “Wives, submit to your own husbands, as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife even as Christ is the head of the church.” The key is the pattern of Christ. Husbands are told, “Love your wives, as Christ loved the church and gave himself up for her, that he might sanctify her.” Headship is defined by sacrificial love. Marriage is a picture of Christ and the church: “This mystery is profound, and I am saying that it refers to Christ and the church.” Christians differ on the application: complementarians understand the passage to describe distinct roles in which husbands lead and wives submit, while egalitarians stress mutual submission in verse 21 and understand headship as source or servant leadership. Both agree that husbands must love sacrificially and that abuse of any kind violates this text.

Children are to obey their parents in the Lord, for it is right, and honor them, the first commandment with a promise. Fathers are not to provoke their children to anger, but to bring them up in the discipline and instruction of the Lord. Slaves are to obey with sincerity, as serving Christ, and masters are to do the same to them, knowing that both have a Master in heaven who shows no partiality. Paul’s teaching undermines the slave system from within.

The letter ends with a call to battle. “Be strong in the Lord and in the strength of his might. Put on the whole armor of God, that you may be able to stand against the schemes of the devil.” The enemy is not human but spiritual. The armor: the belt of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, shoes of the readiness given by the gospel of peace, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God. Almost all of it is defensive; the aim is to stand. And all of it is surrounded by prayer: “praying at all times in the Spirit.” Paul asks for prayer for himself, that he would declare the gospel boldly. The letter ends with peace, love, and grace.
connection: Genesis 2:24 is quoted in 5:31. Exodus 20:12 is quoted in 6:2-3. Isaiah 11:4-5, 52:7, and 59:17 stand behind the armor. 1 Peter 3:1-7 gives parallel household teaching. Colossians 3:18 to 4:1 is a close parallel. Philemon applies the teaching on masters and slaves. Psalm 119 praises the word. 2 Corinthians 10:3-5 describes spiritual warfare. 1 Peter 5:8-9 warns of the devil. Matthew 4:1-11 shows Jesus using the sword of the Spirit. James 4:7 says resist the devil.
application:
Pray through each piece of the armor this week. Name each as you put it on.

If you are married, ask your spouse how you could love them more like Christ. If you are a parent, look for an area where you can bring up your children in the Lord.

Pray for a missionary or pastor who is boldly declaring the gospel.
prayerPrompts: Ask God to help you walk in love as Christ loved you.
Ask him to fill you with his Spirit.
Ask him to help you put on the whole armor of God.
